# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# A Critical Reading of the Two-Year Follow-up of the Varden Trial and Halden Subset

**This is the most informative document in the series, and its rebuttals of the earlier claims are mostly fair.** It addresses the questions left open, in most cases using the standards the critics themselves set. Its central result is a gain of 8.5% in output per hour two years on, randomised and measured from system logs. That is the best single estimate so far, and it fits the meta-analysis's range of roughly 8–10%.

The weaknesses:
- The summary describes the decline over time inconsistently.
- Contamination of the control group, which the authors report, isn't connected to their decay estimate.
- The mediation analysis has some methodological gaps.
- The Halden subset's selection is described somewhat generously.

## The numbers check out

| Item | Check |
|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, system logs | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden subset hours | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a 13.4% fall ✓ |
| Halden subset per hour | 0.968 / 0.866 = 1.118, so +11.8% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓ |
| Counter staffing | 0.83 × 1.067 = 0.886 of baseline output; restoring it needs about 13% more staff, matching the county's 12% ✓ |

## What the follow-up does well

- **It sets its tests before seeing the results.** The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month data existed.
- **It measures hours more strictly.** System logs addressed the concern that timesheets miss unclaimed work. They confirmed that concern, though only slightly: hours fell 11% on logs against 12% on timesheets.
- **It reports results that cut against a reduced-hours story:**
  - the per-hour gain declined;
  - output per employee is below control;
  - the counter arm was stopped;
  - Halden organisations reverted.
- **It makes the right correction to the meta-analysis.** All four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which are exactly the features the review found inflate estimates. Its claim that effects don't decay therefore had no sound basis.
- **It doesn't overclaim from the meeting-audit offices.** It explicitly says whether reorganising work without cutting hours could capture the gain "cannot be determined".
- **It is clear about the Halden subset's limits.** It calls the 11 continuing organisations "survivors twice over" and treats their figure as an upper bound.

## Problems

**1. The summary mixes hours measures when describing the decline.**
The summary says the gain fell "from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a log figure, so the comparison overstates the decline.

| Comparison | Decline |
|---|---|
| Like for like, timesheets (12.5% → 9.8%) | about 22% |
| Mixed measures, as in the summary (12.5% → 8.5%) | about 32% |

Section 5's "about a quarter" falls between the two. The body text gets this right; the summary and Section 5 should match it.

**2. Contamination of the control group may account for part of the "decline".**
Two of the seven control offices cut their meetings at month 15 and raised their own output per hour by about 4.1%.

- If offices are of similar size, that lifts the control average by roughly 1.2 points from month 15 on.
- That narrows the gap between treated and control offices whether or not the treated offices' gain faded.
- So part of the 2.7-point fall (12.5% to 9.8%) may come from control offices improving rather than treated offices declining.

The audit may also have been prompted by awareness of the trial, which would make it a spillover rather than a coincidence. The authors report the audit as an aside but don't connect it to their decay estimate. A sensitivity analysis that excludes or adjusts for those two offices should be reported.

**3. Two time points can't show whether the decline has stopped.**
The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% was not tested statistically, and the two confidence intervals overlap heavily. Even if the decline is real, two points can't distinguish between a gain that has levelled off and one still shrinking slowly. The paper rightly criticises Varga and Holm for extrapolating from two survey points; the same caution applies here. "Declined but not disappeared at 24 months" is accurate. Saying it will persist is not yet justified. The limitations section acknowledges this, but the framing in Section 5 is more confident.

**4. The mediation analysis has several methodological gaps.**
- **Few clusters.** "A larger sample of office-months" makes the analysis sound larger than it is. Repeated months from the same office aren't independent, so there are effectively 14 offices. The confidence interval of 28%–66% may be too narrow, as with the earlier cluster-robust intervals. Again, no small-sample correction is reported.
- **Reverse causation.** Meeting time and output were measured over the same period. Offices that became more productive might simply have needed fewer coordination meetings. Registering the analysis in advance doesn't solve this.
- **What the logs measure is unclear.** "Active log-in time on the case-management system" may or may not include meeting time, and the interpretation depends on which:

| If log hours… | then the meetings result means… |
|---|---|
| include meetings | cutting meetings raises output per hour almost by definition, and the 47% partly reflects that |
| exclude meetings | the gain must work through another route, such as fewer interruptions to case work |

  The logs also miss work done outside the system, such as email and phone. That makes "stricter" true only in one direction: logs capture case work not claimed on timesheets, but not other work.
- **A rough calculation suggests meetings explain even more.**
  - Control offices: about 37.9 actual hours minus 7.0 in meetings leaves about 30.9 hours of other work.
  - Treated offices: about 33.7 actual hours (11% fewer) minus 3.9 in meetings leaves about 29.8 hours.
  - That is about 3.5% less non-meeting time, almost exactly matching the 3.4% fall in output per employee.
  - So if meetings produced little output, output per non-meeting hour barely changed. Cutting meetings would then account for nearly all the gain, not 47%.

  This doesn't invalidate the mediation estimate, which measures something different. But the authors should reconcile the two, and the comparison depends on which hours the logs cover.

**5. The Halden subset is selected more heavily than the report admits.**
- **Who responded.** Only 14 of 23 contacted organisations responded. The nine that didn't are likely to include more reverters.
- **The hours baseline.** The baseline of 40.3 is the 27-organisation figure from Varga and Holm. It's unclear whether these 11 organisations all used time tracking (only 17 of the 23 did) or whether their own baseline was used.
- **How the reversions are described.** The summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations". But one was a marketing agency citing client deadlines, which is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. Stretching "coverage" to fit makes the pattern look neater than it is. A discretionary-sector reversion is worth reporting as such.
- **Possible conflict of interest.** One of the authors wrote the original Halden paper. This doesn't undermine the Varden results, but readers should know it when weighing the Halden section.

**6. Cost is analysed for counters but not for case-processing.**
For counter offices, the county estimated that restoring service would raise cost per contact by 9%. For case-processing, there is no equivalent figure. Pay is unchanged and output per employee is down 3.4%, so cost per case is roughly 3.5% higher. Paid overtime adds to that. Employers need this figure as much as the per-hour gain.

**7. Earlier gaps remain.**
- **Backlogs and deadlines.** Backlog size and compliance with statutory deadlines are still not reported, despite being raised as a concern at nine months.
- **Sick leave.** The rota structure is still not stated, so the −27% fall in sick days may still be partly mechanical.
- **Quality.** Appeal overturn rates are stable (3.2% v 3.0%), but they remain an insensitive measure of quality.

## How the earlier claims stand now

| Claim | Status after this follow-up |
|---|---|
| Halden: +23.4% per hour, model works in all sectors | Not supported: inflated by measurement, and coverage-bound work fails |
| Varga & Holm: gains "entirely an artifact", novelty explains the rest | Not supported: 8.5% remains after randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and two years |
| Varga & Holm: novelty contributes | Partly supported: some decline, though part may reflect control-group contamination |
| Meta-analysis: roughly 8–10% per hour; coverage-bound work loses output per worker | Supported |
| Meta-analysis: no decay, so novelty can be set aside | Not supported: its evidence was weak, and the one controlled long-run study shows some decline |
| Varden: meetings are a substantial mechanism | Supported by a pre-specified test, subject to the gaps in issue 4 |

## Overall

The evidence across all five documents now points to a consistent picture:
- In discretionary work, cutting scheduled hours by 20% reduces actual hours by about 11–13%.
- Output per hour rises by about 8–10% in the best-measured study, and this lasts at least two years, with some decline.
- Output per employee falls slightly, by about 2–4%, so cost per unit of output rises modestly.
- A large part of the gain appears to come from removing low-value meeting time rather than from rest alone.
- In coverage-bound work, the scheme cuts service unless more staff are hired, and the one employer that tested it stopped.

The most important open question is the one the authors raise themselves: whether cutting meetings without cutting hours could capture most of the gain. A trial arm that reorganises work without reducing hours would answer it.
